For a genuinely non-solvable Schrödinger operator, apparently nothing is known. Voros's exact WKB and spectral-determinant functional relations describe E_0 implicitly, so a proof would have to turn those relations, or a series or continued fraction for E_0, into Diophantine information.
notes: The numerical value is correct. I found no literature on the arithmetic nature of E_0; it is novel in the sense of never having been posed explicitly. The statement is precise. There is no realistic route: no available tool gives irrationality of a constant defined only implicitly through a non-solvable ODE. So this is a clean 'benchmark of ignorance' rather than an attackable problem, and the specific choice of x^4 and of E_0 is somewhat arbitrary. Graded B for cleanness, kept below A because it is likely hopeless and not tied to a broader programme.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
W: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
M: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)
why: Joining the c trees with c - 1 new edges makes a single tree, and a graceful labelling of that tree restricts to such a labelling of the forest. So this statement follows from the Graceful Tree Conjecture (Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa) but is weaker than it. The best unconditional results only give labels in {1,...,(1+eps)n}, or (1-eps)n distinct differences, so even one spare label for every tree would be new progress.
notes: The original hypothesis (c >= 2 and one tree with more than m/2 edges) is arbitrary. An exhaustive backtracking search over ALL forests with at most 11 vertices (475 forests at n=11) found a valid labelling for every one, with or without that hypothesis. So the hypothesis is not doing any work, and I replaced it with 'every forest'. The original version already contains the open T + K1 case (one spare label for every tree), so neither version is easy. Novelty is moderate: range-relaxed graceful labellings are studied (Van Bussel 2002; Adamaszek–Allen–Grosu–Hladký; the 2025 gracesize paper), and I did not find this exact forest formulation, but it is a natural reformulation that experts would likely regard as folklore-adjacent.

title: Positive metric entropy for the x^4+y^4 billiard
W: The billiard table x^4 + y^4 <= 1 is smooth and convex, but its curvature vanishes at four points, so (by Mather) it has no caustics. Its phase space mixes stable islands with apparently chaotic regions. Prove that the chaos is real: on a set of positive measure, nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast.
M:
Let $\Phi$ be the billiard map of $\Omega=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$, preserving the Liouville measure $
u=\sin	heta\,ds\,d	heta$. Prove that $h_
u(\Phi)>0$; equivalently, by Pesin's formula, that $\Phi$ has a nonzero Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive $
u$-measure.
why: Proving positive metric entropy for any smooth, area-preserving twist map with coexisting KAM islands, such as the Chirikov standard map, is a central and notoriously hard open problem. No smooth (C^2 or better) convex billiard is known to have positive metric entropy: the known examples, like stadiums and lemons, have boundary singularities. The analytic table x^4 + y^4 = 1 is the most natural concrete test case, and numerics show entropy of about 0.65 there.
notes: Not novel. Knill and coauthors studied exactly the family of billiards in l^p unit balls. They proved positive TOPOLOGICAL entropy for p not in {1, 2, infinity} and found elliptic periodic orbits, so the billiard is not ergodic. Their metric entropy estimates are numerical only, with a peak near p = 4 to 6 of about 0.65. Positive metric entropy is left open there and is a well-known open problem type. Recent progress covers topological entropy (generic analytic convex billiards, 2026; generic convex bodies, 2022) and ergodicity of asymmetric lemons (strictly convex but with corners), none of which settles this. The statement is well-posed; I made the invariant measure explicit and noted the Pesin equivalence. W's 'positive fraction is chaotic' matches 'positive Lyapunov exponent on positive measure'. One URL (Knill's html page) was blocked; the PDF was read.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
W: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)
why: The sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg constant on a cone of angle alpha <= 2*pi should be (alpha/2*pi) times the planar one, with the radial Q as extremiser. If so, conical singularities lower the mass threshold for collapse, and the cube surface turns this into a clean statement with an explicit constant. A proof would test the mass-critical blow-up theory (Weinstein, Merle–Raphaël, Burq–Gérard–Tzvetkov) on singular geometries, where existing Strichartz estimates come with loss.
notes: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted; prior work I know of (Strichartz estimates on flat cones by Ford and by Blair–Ford–Marzuola) was not re-checked. Fixes: specified the self-adjoint realisation, since on 2D cones the Laplacian on functions supported away from the vertex is not essentially self-adjoint because of the log r mode. Also replaced 'blow-up for EVERY m > 3/4||Q||^2' with 'blow-up for masses arbitrarily close above m_*'. That is the honest threshold statement, while arbitrarily large blow-up mass on a compact surface needs a separate argument, so I kept it as an optional strengthening. Part (i) looks fairly routine given a sharp GN inequality on the cone (cones with angle <= 2*pi have apex-centred disks as isoperimetric optimisers, so Polya–Szego symmetrisation should work) plus a local H^1 theory. Part (ii), building near-threshold blow-up concentrating at a vertex, is the real content.

title: Fibonacci-modulated growing Jacobi matrix
W: Take a Jacobi matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal weights sqrt(n). Double the weight at every position where the Fibonacci word has a 1. Periodic modulations of power-growing weights are known to produce spectral phase transitions. Determine the spectral type for this aperiodic modulation.
M: Let $f=f_1f_2f_3\cdots=0100101001001\cdots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ be the Fibonacci word, the fixed point of $0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0$. Let $J$ be the Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $(Ju)_n=a_{n-1}u_{n-1}+a_nu_{n+1}$, where $a_n=\sqrt n\,(1+f_n)$ and $a_0u_0:=0$. Since $\sum 1/a_n=\infty$, $J$ is self-adjoint (Carleman). Determine the spectral type of $J$. In particular: is $\sigma_{ac}(J)\neq\emptyset$? Is $\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$? Is the spectrum on some interval pure point or singular continuous?
why: Janas, Naboko, Swiderski and others classified unbounded Jacobi matrices with periodically modulated power-growing weights. Whether the spectrum is absolutely continuous, a gap, or point spectrum is decided by the trace of a single period's transfer matrix. A Fibonacci modulation joins this theory to the trace-map dynamics of quasicrystal Schrodinger operators. In that setting the period matrix is replaced by a hierarchy of block products.
notes: I found no literature on aperiodic or Sturmian modulations of unbounded weights, only periodic ones (Janas-Naboko, Swiderski, Naboko-Simonov). Heuristic: with b=0 and lambda/a_n -> 0, two-step transfer matrices are close to diag(-a_{n-1}/a_n, -a_{n-2}/a_{n-1}). Their products are governed by D_N=sum_{k<=N}(f_{2k-1}-f_{2k}). Numerically |D_N| grows like log N (records +-10 by N=10^6, about one unit per factor phi^3), so 2^{D_N} is roughly N^{0.47}. That is close to the l^2 borderline, and it competes with the O(sqrt N) phase rotation from lambda/a_n. So the answer is not obvious. I fixed the indexing and the convention for the Fibonacci word, and added the self-adjointness remark. The choices of exponent 1/2 and factor 2 are somewhat arbitrary.

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
W: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
M: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.
why: Ergodicity of billiards in irrational polygons is open even in the plane. No explicit irrational triangle is known to be ergodic, although Kerckhoff-Masur-Smillie and Vorobets show that generic polygons are. The regular tetrahedron is the most symmetric and canonical non-rational polyhedron, so it is the natural first test case for polyhedral billiards. In that setting the group generated by reflection linear parts is infinite, which rules out the translation-surface methods.
notes: Open as far as I can tell. The literature on tetrahedral billiards covers periodic orbits (Fagnano-type orbits, Bedaride and others) and 'uniformity' results for special polyhedra built from 2D (Beck et al.). I found nothing on ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron. The statement is clean. I added the treatment of singular orbits. Caveat: this is probably far beyond current techniques, since even a single explicit ergodic irrational triangle is unknown. A related, perhaps more tractable variant: is the flow topologically transitive, or are there only countably many periodic directions?

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
W: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.
M: Let $S=\partial K$ for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ with smooth boundary and positive Gaussian curvature, and let $d$ be the intrinsic distance on $S$. Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.
why: This is the Toeplitz square peg problem moved from the plane to intrinsic geometry. In the plane the smooth case is classical (Schnirelmann), and there are strong recent results (Greene-Lobb rectangles). Recent work extends inscription theorems to constant-curvature surfaces: the hyperbolic plane, and spheres for curves disjoint from their antipodal image. A general convex surface tests whether the topological parity argument survives variable curvature and a non-smooth distance function (cut loci).
notes: Original M said 'geodesic quadrilateral' without defining it, and it did not exclude degenerate squares or fix the cyclic order. I fixed all three. I found no paper treating general convex surfaces. Naseri Sadr 2025 covers the constant-curvature cases (could not open the page to check details). For curves inside a strongly convex geodesic ball the standard Schnirelmann parity argument probably adapts. The real difficulty is long curves whose would-be diagonals cross the cut locus, where d is not smooth. Likely true. Moderate interest.

title: Euler with reversed stretching
W: Flip the sign of the vortex-stretching term in the 3D Euler vorticity equation and keep advection and the Biot-Savart law. Do smooth solutions stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?
M:
On $\mathbb T^3$ let $\omega:\mathbb T^3	imes[0,T)	o\mathbb R^3$ solve $\partial_t\omega+(u\cdot
abla)\omega=-S\omega$, where $u=
abla	imes(-\Delta)^{-1}(\omega-\langle\omegaangle)$, $S=	frac12(
abla u+
abla u^{T})$ and $\langle\omegaangle$ is the spatial mean. Decide whether every $\omega_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $
abla\cdot\omega_0=0$ generates a global smooth solution.
why: Advection and vortex stretching are the same size under scaling, and their competition decides regularity in 1D Euler models. In the De Gregorio, Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos and Okamoto-Sakajo-Wunsch models, the sign and relative weight of stretching flip the answer between blow-up and regularity (Elgindi-Jeong). This is the full 3D analogue: it isolates the sign of stretching while keeping the true nonlocal Biot-Savart structure.
notes: Fixes: (1) The reversed equation does NOT preserve div omega = 0 (one computes (d_t+u.grad)div omega = -2 d_i u_j d_j omega_i + ...), so curl u != omega in general and the system is only a model. (2) The mean of omega is not conserved (d/dt mean = -int S omega), so (-Delta)^{-1} must act on the mean-free part. I fixed M accordingly. Observation: for axisymmetric swirl-free data, div omega = 0 is preserved and r*omega_theta (not omega_theta/r as in true Euler) is transported. So omega_theta can grow as fluid moves toward the axis. This is a natural first test case, and it hints that the answer may differ from true Euler. I found no 3D paper on exactly this model, only 1D analogues.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
W: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
M: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)
why: Khalfalah and Szemeredi proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic pair x != y with x+y a square; this asks for the next configuration, a monochromatic triangle in the 'square-sum graph'. Density arguments fail (residue classes such as n = 1 mod 3 contain no such triangle), so a proof must be genuinely Ramsey-theoretic, in the same family as the open Pythagorean-triple and {x,y,x+y,xy} problems.
notes: Statement clean; colouring renamed to chi to avoid a clash with the element c. Not found posed in the literature (checked Khalfalah-Szemeredi line, Pach's x+y=z^2 work, Di Nasso-Luperi Baglini style surveys). Local (p-adic) obstructions do not kill it: for each prime one residue/valuation class survives. Quick SAT check (CaDiCaL): a 2-colouring of {1..8000} avoiding such triangles exists, but none exists for {1..10000}, so the r=2 case holds with threshold in (8000,10000]; r>=3 is open computationally. Natural but somewhat specialised; B.

title: Computable connective constants
W: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
M: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?
why: The connective constant is the basic growth rate of self-avoiding walks; for graphs with a (unimodular) graph height function, bridge counts are supermultiplicative and give matching lower bounds, so mu is computable for e.g. solvable groups with solvable word problem. Whether this can fail when no height function exists (Higman-type groups, torsion groups such as Grigorchuk's) ties the probabilistic theory of SAWs on groups to computability and symbolic dynamics, where entropies of effective subshifts are exactly the right-computable reals.
notes: Statement precise; inf=lim holds by submultiplicativity on transitive graphs. Known: mu is right computable for recursively presented groups (Aubrun-Bitar 2023, cited as Lemma 4.11 in arXiv 2402.13944); log mu is the entropy of the SAW 'skeleton' subshift; computable (Perron-number powers) for plain groups; lower bounds via bridges for Cayley graphs with graph height functions (Grimmett-Li), covering all f.g. solvable groups. The general question (left-computability without height functions) does not appear posed. A negative answer would need a group with solvable word problem whose SAW growth encodes a non-computable left limit, plausible via Dehn-monster or torsion constructions; neither direction looks easy. Specialised audience; B.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
W: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
M: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).
why: Point-vortex systems are the standard finite-dimensional models of 2D Euler; integrability is classified on the plane, sphere and for zero total circulation on the torus, but for nonzero circulation on the torus the translation momenta do not commute and only N=2 is integrable. Proving non-integrability for N=3 identical vortices would be the first rigorous chaos result for vortex lattices, where only numerics (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin) exist.
notes: W's premise was false for identical vortices: Stremler-Aref integrability of three vortices in a periodic parallelogram requires zero total circulation; with nonzero total circulation only N=2 is integrable (survey arXiv 2003.00716, Thm 7) and N=3 is numerically nonintegrable (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin, RCD 2019). Hence the original 'four identical' version skipped the first open case; restated with N=3 as main case. Clarified the reduction: Z in T is a genuine conserved quantity, translation by 1/N-lattice points acts on its level set, reduced dimension 2N-2 (P_x,P_y do not Poisson-commute, so translations remove only one degree of freedom). Also fixed Green-function normalisation (uniform background). Likely approach: Ziglin/Morales-Ramis along a collinear or symmetric invariant family, or Melnikov splitting; technical but feasible.

title: Translative Lebesgue covering: area constant
W: Only translations allowed: find the least area of a convex shape that contains a translated copy of every planar set of diameter 1. It is known that this area lies between sqrt(3)/2 ~ 0.866 (the regular hexagon of width 1 is forced) and pi/3 ~ 1.047 (Jung's disc). Improve either bound.
M: sqrt3/2 <= alpha <= pi/3 (unchanged; replace the 'even' step with D3-invariance plus convexity)
why: Lebesgue's universal-cover problem (rigid motions allowed) is a century old and still unsolved; the translation-only version is the natural rigid analogue of Pal's solution of the convex Kakeya problem (equilateral triangle of height 1) and of Bezdek-Connelly's theorem that the disc of radius 1/sqrt3 is the unique minimum-perimeter translation cover of diameter-1 sets. Its answer measures how much rotation actually helps in Lebesgue's problem.
notes: No prior area result for translation covers of diameter-1 sets found (2608.30538 treats rigid motions only). Lower bound sqrt3/2 derived here, numerically checked (hull of R and -R = hexagon). Earlier numerics suggest alpha<pi/3.
bound: alpha = least area of a convex set containing a translate of every planar set of diameter 1

alpha >= sqrt(3)/2 ~ 0.8660 (new, self-contained): K contains translates R+a and -R+b of the Reuleaux triangle R; f(t)=area conv(R u (-R+t)) is convex in t (Rogers-Shephard 1958, Lemma 1, linear parameter systems) and even (f(-t)=f(t) by x->-x then translation), so min at t=0, where conv(R u -R) is the regular hexagon of width 1, area sqrt(3)/2. Beats trivial pi/4 (disc of diameter 1).
alpha <= pi/3 ~ 1.0472: disc of radius 1/sqrt3 (Jung's theorem); this disc is the unique minimum-perimeter translation cover (Bezdek-Connelly), but nothing better for area is known.

title: Spikes at the primes
W: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
M: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?
why: It is the cleanest deterministic test of whether the primes are 'pseudo-random' for spectral theory: the random sparse model with site density 1/log n localizes, while deterministic sparse potentials typically produce singular continuous spectrum. The answer must use arithmetic input (distribution of primes in residue classes and gaps), linking Schrodinger operators to analytic number theory.
notes: No absolutely continuous spectrum is automatic: 1_P takes finitely many values and is not eventually periodic, so Remling's theorem (Annals 2011) gives Sigma_ac = empty; hence the content is pure point vs singular continuous. The conjectured pure-point answer is doubtful: numerics in the 2001 study 'De(Localization) in the Prime Schrodinger Operator' (cond-mat/0103313) report a persistent delocalized band near E=0 of width ~1/lambda. Simple check: at E=0 the recursion decouples by parity and, since all primes but 2 are odd, solutions grow only like partial sums of chi_4(p) (polynomially), not like the random model; analogous arithmetic resonances occur at E=2cos(pi a/q). So 'prove pure point' was replaced by 'determine the spectral type'. The question is posed (numerically) in the literature, so novelty is low; difficulty likely very high. Literature search for rigorous results was cut short by the search budget.

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
W: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
M: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ be $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic with $\int_{[0,1]^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. Test case: $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos(2\pi x)$ (equivalently $a=\cos x$ with $2\pi$-periodicity).
why: Fujita's theorem is the prototype of 'all solutions blow up vs. small data global' thresholds; with a sign-changing, mean-zero weight the first-order effect cancels and the threshold is set by a homogenized second-order term $c\,v^{2p-1}$ with $c=\langle a,(-\Delta)^{-1}a\rangle>0$, predicting $p^*=1+1/d$. The posed equation is exactly the critical case $d=1,p=2$, where standard test-function/Kaplan arguments fail because the weight changes sign.
notes: red team: No literature on mean-zero periodic weights; Pinsky and Kawakami-Sire-Wang assume a>=0. But the near-identity change u=w+phi w^p seems to make (ii) routine: crude decay bounds on the new terms are integrable exactly when p>1+1/d. Subcritical blowup is plausibly within reach of test-function methods. Only the critical case looks hard. A nice but likely-routine niche Fujita variant, so B.

title: Minimal degree of a Jacobian counterexample
W: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpöge's map has component degrees 7,6,4). Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. Find the smallest degree a three-variable counterexample can have: some number from 3 to 7.
M: Call $F\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]^3$ a Keller map if $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, and set $\deg F=\max_i\deg F_i$. Let $d_3=\min\{\deg F: F\text{ Keller, not injective on }\mathbb C^3\}$. Known: $3\le d_3\le 7$. Improve either bound: exhibit a non-injective Keller map with $\deg F\le 6$, or prove $d_3\ge 4$ (equivalently, every Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ of degree $\le3$ is invertible), or determine $d_3$.
why: Now that the Jacobian conjecture is known to fail in dimension 3, the obvious next question is how small a failure can be. The minimal degree marks the line between low-degree regimes where invertibility can still be proved (Wang's degree-2 theorem, cubic-homogeneous results in small dimension) and the region where counterexamples exist. Because the Bass–Connell–Wright reduction raises the dimension, the cubic case in dimension 3 is a genuinely separate question.
notes: The original said 'the 2026 counterexamples have degree 7'. That is accurate for Alpöge's F (7,6,4) and van den Essen's (7,5,4), but Gallagher-type examples have higher degree, so I reworded it to 'degree 7 at best'. I defined 'Keller map' and 'degree' (max component degree, as opposed to geometric degree) and stated the known bounds 3<=d_3<=7. I found no paper that determines d_3 or settles the general cubic case in C^3, but the question is probably being actively studied. It is also a finite-dimensional algebraic problem for each degree, so computer searches may settle it soon, which lowers its long-term novelty.

title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up: the exponent
W: Glue regular tetrahedra face to face in a chain of length n; it can never close exactly. How close to closing can it get? Short arguments show the best gap is at least about 3^{-n/2} and, for infinitely many n, at most about 3^{-n/12}; counting suggests 3^{-n/6}. Narrow the exponent range [1/12, 1/2].
M: With kappa:=liminf -(1/n)log_3 min_{k<=n} g(k) (or kappa:=limsup with exact length): 1/12 <= kappa <= 1/2
why: Steinhaus's tetrahedral-chain problem asks whether a ring can close. It is a concrete free-product subgroup of the isometry group with all entries in Z[1/3]. The rotation parts behave like the Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak quaternions of norm 3^n. The near-closure rate is therefore an optimal-approximation question in an S-arithmetic group acting on R^3, combining a Ramanujan-type rotation part with a translation part that behaves like a random walk.
notes: Both bounds derived here (lower improves the q0 record's 3^{-n}); primitivity verified numerically to n=11. Literature gives only qualitative non-closure and experiments (Elgersma-Wagon: eps with ~10 log(1/eps) tetrahedra, i.e. kappa>~0.09, consistent).
bound: kappa = liminf_{n} -(1/n) log_3 g(n), g(n)= min Hausdorff distance between T_n and T_0 over non-backtracking face-reflection chains of length n

g(n) >= c*3^{-n/2} for all n (new, short proof): g_n = s_{i1}...s_{in}, linear part = ±R_q, q = v_{i1}...v_{in}, v_i the pure quaternions ±i±j±k (norm 3); non-backtracking => q primitive in the Hurwitz order (unique factorisation; checked by computer to n=11). If T_n is near T_0 the linear part is near a symmetry ±R_u; q*conj(u) cannot be real (primitivity / 2*3^n not a square), so its vector part has length >=1/2 while |q u| <= sqrt2*3^{n/2}, giving rotation error >> 3^{-n/2}. Hence kappa <= 1/2.

pigeonhole: 4*3^{m-1} chains of length m have endpoint isometries in a 6-dim region of volume poly(m); two lie within 3^{-m/6+o(m)}; A followed by reversed B is a reduced nonempty chain of length <=2m (nonzero by Swierczkowski/Dekker/Mason non-closure). So g(n) <= 3^{-n/12+o(n)} for infinitely many n, i.e. kappa >= 1/12.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
W: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
M: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.
why: Standard mKdV on the torus is globally well-posed because L² conservation and the L²-subcritical Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality control the energy. A spatially varying coefficient breaks the translation symmetry and so the L² law, which removes the a priori bound. Any blow-up would have to come from L² growth rather than L² concentration. That is a mechanism of real interest for inhomogeneous dispersive equations, and this is about the simplest model where it could occur.
notes: I checked the conservation laws: ∫u is a Casimir and H is the Hamiltonian, while d/dt||u||² = (1/2)∫ sin x u⁴, so L² can grow. The a priori estimates close only into dM/dt ≲ M³, which does not rule out blow-up. The weighted mass ∫|cos x|^{1/3}u² cancels the quartic term in the Kato identity, but that weight is singular at the zeros of cos, so it gives no global bound. Numerics (Fourier, N=512, integrating-factor RK4, dt=1e-5, initial data 3exp(-4(x-π/2)²)) conserve H=11.28 to 4 digits while ||u||² grows from 6.4 to 12.7 by t=0.8. The coarser run dt=2e-5 reached 23.9 at t=1.0 and then lost resolution. That growth is consistent with blow-up but does not establish it. Cos x is one arbitrary choice, and the same question makes sense for any sign-changing smooth coefficient a(x). I could not finish the literature check because the web-search budget ran out; work on inhomogeneous gKdV exists, but I could not check whether this case is covered.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
W: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
M: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.
why: Which graphs are common (random coloring is optimal) is a central question in Ramsey multiplicity. The known obstructions (containing $K_4$, the Turán-coloring criterion of Fox–Wigderson) do not apply to the triangle-free, girth-5, 3-chromatic Petersen graph. It is a natural test case, between odd cycles (common) and graphs containing $K_4$ (uncommon).
notes: Original 'determine the constant' rewritten as the commonness question; if P is common the constant is 2^{-14}. Checks: P has no K4, so Thomason's obstruction does not apply. Its smallest even subgraph with min degree 2 is C6, and t(C6,U)>=0, so P passes the first local-commonness test. Turán colorings give 32-560 times the random value. A random search over 2- to 4-step graphons found nothing below 2^{-14} (best 1.035x). Found no paper settling P.

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
W: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
M: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).
why: Kozlov's theorem rules out first integrals that are analytic in ε for generic trigonometric perturbations of the flat torus. Proving non-integrability at each fixed ε, uniformly down to ε→0, needs control of exponentially small splitting at resonances. This is an explicit test of that gap.
notes: Wrote out the metric explicitly. The ε-analytic (Poincaré–Kozlov) version follows from Kozlov because the Fourier spectrum of the perturbation is not on a line. The fixed-ε statement for all ε>0 seems open but is quite specific. By Paternain/Taimanov, positive topological entropy would be enough.

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
W: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
M: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
why: Huang's proof is a short spectral argument, interlacing for a signed adjacency matrix. Asking whether weak proof systems can capture it tests how much linear algebra cutting planes and SOS can simulate. It belongs to the programme of locating famous combinatorial theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy.
notes: Checked the sizes: the formula has size N^{1+o(1)}, and Huang's bound gives unsatisfiability exactly at d=ceil(sqrt n)-1. Part (a) is probably 'no' for routine pigeonhole/matching reasons: even the d=0 case (an independent set larger than N/2) is a matching-type principle that is hard for resolution. That case is easy in cutting planes via a perfect matching. So (b) and (c) are the real content, and the W wording should stress them. Found no prior work on this.

title: Hat Ising universality
W: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
M: Let $G$ be the planar graph whose vertices are the tiles of a fixed hat tiling (Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss), with edges between tiles sharing a boundary segment. Consider the ferromagnetic nearest-neighbour Ising model on $G$ with uniform coupling $J=1$. Prove that there is a critical $\beta_c$ (independent of the tiling in the hull), and that as $\beta\to\beta_c$ the spontaneous magnetization, susceptibility and correlation length obey $M(\beta)\asymp(\beta-\beta_c)^{1/8}$, $\chi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-7/4}$, $\xi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-1}$.
why: Rigorous 2D Ising universality is known for isoradial graphs at Z-invariant weights and for periodic graphs. Uniform couplings on an aperiodic, non-isoradial graph are not covered. The hat graph is a canonical such test, and numerics (Matsubara–Suzuki) support universality.
notes: Original M did not say which graph, which couplings, or which definitions of the exponents. Fixed: tile-adjacency graph, uniform J, and asymptotics up to constants. Existing work is Monte Carlo only, with ν and β assumed rather than fitted. This is an instance of the broader open problem of universality for quasiperiodic planar Ising models.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
M:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=\Delta u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ loses smoothness in finite time.
why: Steady stirring is the physically basic forcing, and a time-independent force cannot be tuned to the scales of a developing singularity. A positive answer would mean the singularity is produced by the nonlinearity alone under a fixed energy input. A negative answer would show that the time-dependent forcing in known constructions is essential.
notes: Before 2026 this was a strengthening of Clay's forced statement. After OpenAI's claimed time-dependent forced blow-up (force supported away from $t=0$, not yet refereed) it is the natural next step. Only gradient forces are excluded trivially, since they give the zero solution (Cao–Chi–Nie Prop. 3.17), so $f$ must have a nontrivial solenoidal part. Heuristic: a bounded steady force is subcritical at small scales, so near the singular point the blow-up is essentially unforced. This is probably far harder than the time-dependent case and close to Millennium level, which limits its value as a list item. I changed the wording to 'decide'.

title: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
W: Sorting an array promised to avoid a fixed pattern needs at least log2 of the number of allowed orders comparisons, and Fredman's theorem says 2n more always suffice. How many extra comparisons per element are really needed? Show that fewer than 2n extra suffice for 1324-avoiding inputs, or show that a linear excess is necessary for some pattern.
M: For a permutation $\tau$ let $C_\tau(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing $\tau$) that sorts $a_1,\dots,a_n$ under the promise that their order pattern lies in $\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)$. Let $\delta_\tau=\limsup_n (C_\tau(n)-\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|)/n$. Known: $0\le\delta_\tau\le2$ (Fredman). Improve either bound for some $\tau$ of length 4, in particular prove $\delta_{1324}<2$, or find $\tau$ with $\delta_\tau>0$. Is $\delta_\tau=0$ for every $\tau$?
why: The comparison model is one of the few settings where information-theoretic lower bounds are often nearly exact. Even for unrestricted sorting it is unknown whether $\log_2 n!+o(n)$ comparisons suffice. Pattern classes give a family where this question is harder to dismiss. A linear gap for some $\tau$ would need a new lower-bound technique, and tightness for every $\tau$ would need a strong structural sorting algorithm.
notes: Opler's abstract checked: it gives no additive-excess constant. Generic Fredman excess cannot be improved for arbitrary sets of permutations, so any delta<2 needs class structure. The upper side for specific length-4 patterns may be moderately accessible.
bound: delta_tau = limsup_n (C_tau(n) - log2|Av_n(tau)|)/n, e.g. tau=1324
delta_tau >= 0: information-theoretic bound C_tau(n) >= log2|Av_n(tau)| (trivial).

delta_tau <= 2: Fredman (1976), any set G of permutations can be sorted with log2|G| + 2n comparisons. Opler (arXiv 2409.07868) gives O((log c_tau +1)n), optimal only up to a constant factor. delta_tau = 0 is known for tau of length 3 in the 132-class (stack sorting, <=2n vs log2 C_n = 2n - O(log n)).

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.
notes: Belk–Hyde–Moore (arXiv:2211.05825) give an explicit rational map with $\rho=\sqrt2-1$, refuting Calegari's question. Their Questions 3–4 are close relatives (deciding for the family $f_{q,r}$, and finite order in $T_q$) but not this exact question, and I found no paper posing it. The c.e. direction checks out. $\rho$ is computable, which only helps for a fixed candidate $p/q$. The statement is clean; I added the encoding and the c.e. justification.

title: Derivative loss in L4 Strichartz on the cube surface
W: On the flat torus, the L4 space-time estimate for Schrodinger waves loses only epsilon derivatives (Bourgain). On the surface of a cube, which has eight cone points that diffract waves, only a loss of 1/4 derivative is known. Find the true loss: prove any loss below 1/4, or show some loss is necessary.
M: Let $S$ be the unit cube surface, $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\text{vertices})$, and $s^*=\inf\{s\ge0:\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_s\|f\|_{H^s(S)}\}$. Known: $0\le s^*\le\tfrac14$ (Blair–Ford–Marzuola). Prove $s^*<\tfrac14$, or $s^*>0$; ideally determine $s^*$ (conjecturally $0$).
why: The cube surface is an arithmetic surface with cone points. Its 'nonsingular' eigenfunctions lift to trigonometric polynomials (Greif–Kaplan–Strichartz–Wiese), but the singular ones are not explicit, and diffraction at the vertices spoils the lattice-counting proof used on the torus. Blair–Ford–Marzuola obtain a $1/p$ loss on all compact flat cone surfaces and suggest the loss is an artefact of their method. The cube is the simplest test case where arithmetic structure and diffraction compete.
notes: Bound version gives partial-progress target; upper bound verified in BFM Thm 1.5. Lower bound only trivial, so gap is the whole interval [0,1/4].
bound: s* = inf{s>=0 : ||e^{itDelta}f||_{L^4([0,1]xS)} <= C||f||_{H^s(S)}} for S the flat cube surface (Friedrichs Laplacian)
s* >= 0 (trivial). No positive lower bound known.
s* <= 1/4: Blair-Ford-Marzuola, Thm 1.5 (arXiv 1003.0666), loss 1/p for compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, p=q=4; authors call the loss an artifact of the method.

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
W: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
M: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.
why: Corvaja and Zannier used the Subspace Theorem to show that the greatest prime factor of the product xy over Markov pairs tends to infinity. The single-number version is the natural strengthening. It sits next to the uniqueness conjecture, where Markov numbers that are prime powers are already handled, and to recent strong-approximation work on the Markoff surface.
notes: I found no proof. Single branches are easy: for example, the branch of odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers follows from primitive-divisor theorems. The difficulty is uniformity over the whole tree. Counting does not decide it: there are about (log X)^2 Markov numbers up to X but (log X)^{|S|} S-units, so counting rules out nothing once |S|>=2. A computer check of the 576 Markov numbers up to 1e24 found nothing surprising (smallest largest prime factors above 1000: 53, 61, 109, ...). I did not confirm whether Corvaja-Zannier state the single-number case as open, so novelty is uncertain. The M was made explicit (definition of the set, convention P(1)=1).

title: Ringel for forests
W: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
M: Prove that for every $m\ge1$ and every forest $F$ with $m$ edges, $E(K_{2m+1})$ can be partitioned into $2m+1$ subgraphs each isomorphic to $F$. Stronger form: every such $F$ admits an injective map $f:V(F)\to\mathbb Z_{2m+1}$ whose edge lengths $\min(|f(u)-f(v)|,\,2m+1-|f(u)-f(v)|)$ are exactly $1,\dots,m$ (a $\rho$-labelling).
why: Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov and Keevash-Staden proved Ringel's conjecture for large trees. Their rainbow-copy and cyclic-shift framework does not need connectivity, but the embedding steps do. So the question is whether connectivity is essential to Ringel-type decompositions. A positive answer would be a natural forest analogue of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa theorem.
notes: No counterexample found. A backtracking search found rho-labellings (and hence cyclic decompositions of K_{2m+1}) for all forests without isolated vertices with m<=9 edges (2, 4, 8, 16, 34, 71, 154, 341 forests). I found no paper stating or proving the forest version: MPS, Keevash-Staden and the Glock-Kuhn-Osthus survey treat only trees. A large-m proof may be an adaptation of the existing machinery, which caps the importance. The M was made precise and the rho-labelling strengthening added.

title: Two-frequency localization
W: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
M: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).
why: Multi-frequency localization at large coupling is known only for a full-measure set of frequency vectors, because the proofs (Bourgain-Goldstein, Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag) delete frequencies by semi-algebraic elimination. Proving it for one explicit Diophantine vector such as (√2,√3), which is Diophantine by Schmidt's subspace theorem, would require an arithmetic way to control double resonances, as Jitomirskaya's method does for one frequency.
notes: This is a special case of a recognised open problem (fixed-frequency localization for multi-frequency analytic potentials), not a new question. arXiv 2603.07180 says it is unknown whether some Diophantine frequency can be fixed, and solves only the dual perturbative regime on Z^d. Eliasson (Acta Math 1997) gives pure point spectrum at fixed Diophantine frequency for large Gevrey/analytic couplings, but without exponential decay of eigenfunctions, so the exponential decay is the open content. The original fixed coupling 10 was arbitrary: every known method gives an inexplicit lambda_0, so I replaced it with 'all lambda >= lambda_0'.

title: Jacobi matrix of primes
W: Build an infinite tridiagonal (Jacobi) matrix with zero diagonal and the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, ... on the off-diagonals. The standard criteria for purely absolutely continuous spectrum need the off-diagonal sequence to vary regularly, and they just fail because prime gaps fluctuate. Decide whether the spectrum is nevertheless purely absolutely continuous on the whole real line.
M: Let $J$ be the self-adjoint Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ given by $(Ju)_n=p_{n-1}u_{n-1}+p_nu_{n+1}$ (with $p_0u_0:=0$), where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime. It is self-adjoint by Carleman's criterion, since $\sum1/p_n=\infty$. Decide whether $\sigma(J)=\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$ with no singular part.
why: Unbounded Jacobi matrices with weights $a_n\to\infty$ and $b_n=0$ have purely absolutely continuous spectrum under bounded-variation conditions on $a_{n+1}/a_n$ (Janas-Naboko, Clark). For the primes, the variation of $p_{n+1}/p_n$ diverges like $\sum g_n/p_n$. A Prüfer heuristic suggests the real obstruction is the oscillatory series $\sum(-1)^n g_n/p_n\,e^{i\phi_n}$ ($g_n$ the prime gaps), so the spectral type appears to encode a parity-of-index statistic of prime gaps.
notes: I did not settle it. At E=0 the eigenvector equation is solvable exactly: $u_{2k+1}/u_1=(-1)^k\prod p_{2j-1}/p_{2j}$. The two solutions are balanced, both about $p_n^{-1/2}$, exactly when $S_N=\sum_{n\le N}(-1)^ng_n/p_n$ stays bounded. Numerically $S_N\to-0.451$ (checked to $p\approx2\cdot10^7$), and the alternating gap sum $A_N=\sum(-1)^ng_n$ behaves like $\pm0.5\sqrt N\log p_N$. A proof probably needs $A_N=O(N^{1-\delta})$, which looks unproven unconditionally. The answer is therefore likely 'yes', with an unconditional proof possibly out of reach. Second-order terms are controlled unconditionally by Heath-Brown's $\sum g_n^2\ll x^{23/18+\epsilon}$. Literature check was limited because the web-search budget ran out: I found no paper on this matrix but could not complete the search. I rewrote the M to give the operator explicitly.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
W: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
M: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?
why: Uniqueness of jigsaw reconstruction is a well-studied model problem for shotgun assembly (Mossel–Ross; Bordenave–Feige–Mossel; Nenadov–Pfister–Steger), but all known thresholds concern random puzzles, where about n edge types are needed. Since unique assembly forces all n^2 pieces to be distinct, a simple count gives k(n) ≥ c√n, so the question is whether designed puzzles can beat random ones by a polynomial factor, a rigidity/design question in the spirit of de Bruijn tori.
notes: Original M was ambiguous: whether identical pieces count as interchangeable (unlabelled multiset, where swapping identical pieces is not a new assembly) changes the answer completely; fixed to distinct physical pieces, which forces all pieces distinct and gives the counting lower bound k(n) ≥ c n^{1/2}. Random-puzzle results give k(n) ≤ (1+o(1))n. Found no deterministic-design result. The unlabelled variant (constant k possible?) is a separate, also interesting question, related to tile-complexity results in self-assembly. Risk: an explicit coordinate-encoding construction may give Θ(√n) fairly routinely.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
W: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
M: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.
why: Jörgens' theorem and its extensions (Calabi, Pogorelov; Yuan's work on special Lagrangian equations) depend on the Monge–Ampère or Lagrangian structure, which allows Lewy or Legendre-type transformations to linear or holomorphic problems. The permanent level set {ac+b²=1} is a one-sheeted hyperboloid. It is not a symplectic Monge–Ampère equation, its ellipticity degenerates both at infinity and at the finite boundary 2b²=1, and in two dimensions Liouville theorems are known in general only for uniformly elliptic F (Nirenberg). So this is a clean test of whether 2D Bernstein–Jörgens rigidity needs the special structure.
notes: Checked ellipticity: the symbol [[u_yy,u_xy],[u_xy,u_xx]] is positive definite iff u_xx>0 and u_xx u_yy - u_xy² = 1 - 2u_xy² > 0, so the stated conditions are right and imply convexity. Ruled out simple non-quadratic candidates: separable u=f(x)+g(y)+bxy; u=φ(x)+yψ(x)+y²χ(x) (forces χ ∝ x^{1/3}, not entire); quadratic plus a plane wave f(αx+βy) (forces u_xy² = 1, not elliptic). The equation is not of symplectic Monge–Ampère type (not linear in the Plücker coordinates (1,a,b,c,ac-b²)), so no Sp(4) reduction to Jörgens. The partial Legendre transform gives 2v_py² - v_pp v_yy = v_pp², not linear. Found no literature on this equation; known 2D Liouville theorems (Li–Liang, Nirenberg) need uniform ellipticity, which fails here.

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
W: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
M: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.
why: The ABC flow with A=B=C=1 is the standard model of Lagrangian chaos in steady Euler flows and of fast-dynamo theory, yet rigorous results on its dynamics are mostly perturbative (near integrable parameters) or about non-contractible orbits. Etnyre–Ghrist and Enciso–Peralta-Salas proved that some steady Euler or Beltrami flows realize all knots, using perturbations or random high-frequency fields. Proving it for this explicit lowest-frequency field would most likely need a computer-assisted horseshoe plus template theory (Birman–Williams), turning numerical evidence of chaos into topological information.
notes: Clarified knot type for orbits in T^3 by requiring them to lie in an embedded ball (null-homotopy alone does not give a well-defined classical knot type). Literature: Etnyre–Ghrist (math-ph/9906021) start from the ABC field with A=1, B=1/2, C=0 perturbed, and transplant a horseshoe to a metric on S^3, not the symmetric ABC on T^3. Dombre et al. and arXiv 1601.02724 give periodic orbits with rotation vectors along the axes (non-contractible). Szumiński–Llibre (2609.17449) is perturbative near the axes. Enciso–Peralta-Salas–Romaniega (2006.15033) handle random high-frequency Beltrami fields. Found no result on knotted contractible orbits of the A=B=C=1 flow. Likely approachable by rigorous numerics, so more a hard technical target than a conceptual breakthrough.

title: Beyond the D <= N^{0.172} wall for thin matrix products
W: AVW's core subroutine computes requested entries of XY (N x D times D x N, D <= N^{eps}) in N^2/D^{c} operations; Majdoddin extends the regime to eps < ln4/(5 ln5) ~ 0.17227, matching Coppersmith's 1982 exponent for the same tensor. Either (a) extend the thin-product theorem to some eps > 0.17227 (e.g. via a different base identity, or settle Majdoddin's open thin product <34,2,35>), giving 3SUM/APSP exponents below 1.9945 / 2.9945; or (b) prove that every partial-product-tensor/Coppersmith-style scheme is limited to eps <= 0.17227.
M: Let eps* be the sup of eps such that, for D<=N^eps, any prescribed N^2/sqrt(D) entries of XY (X in Z^{N x D}, Y in Z^{D x N}, poly-bounded entries) can be computed in N^2/D^{gamma} word-RAM operations for some gamma=gamma(eps)>0. Majdoddin shows eps*>=ln4/(5 ln5)~0.17227. (a) Prove eps*>0.17227 (e.g. a base identity such as the thin product <34,2,35>, left open by Majdoddin), or (b) prove that no scheme in a precisely defined class (exact/border partial-product identities with shared inner variable, recursed as in AVW/Majdoddin) exceeds 0.17227.
why: The refutation is real but the saving is tiny (n^{0.0055}); whether it is a crack or a collapse is the key question post-October 2026.
notes: red team: Core question open and posed by Majdoddin arXiv:2610.17420 (<34,2,35> open; App. A already has partial barriers, so (b) is partly done). But the stated payoff is stale: 3SUM is already O(n^1.965) without matrix multiplication (Chan-Itakura-Ma-Yu, Nov 2026), and better exponents come from larger gamma, not larger eps. Narrow technical question, not A.
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D<=N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026)
Coppersmith, Rapid multiplication of rectangular matrices, SICOMP 1982

title: Hinted OMv outside the thin regime
W: For the van den Brand-Nanongkai-Saranurak hinted Mv conjectures (v-hinted Mv, Mv-hinted Mv, uMv-hinted uMv) with hint dimension n^tau, give a polynomially faster algorithm for some tau >= 0.1204 (ideally tau = 1/2), or prove one of them equivalent to plain Boolean OMv for tau >= some explicit threshold.
M: For the vdBNS19 v-hinted Mv and Mv-hinted Mv conjectures with hint dimension n^tau, give an algorithm with polynomial saving for some tau>=0.17227 (ideally tau~0.53, the range used for the dynamic matrix inverse lower bounds), or prove the conjecture at some tau is equivalent to plain OMv.
why: AVW refute these conjectures only for tau < 1/18 (smaller savings up to tau < 0.1204). The phase transition between refuted and unrefuted is now an explicit, checkable frontier.
notes: red team: As stated it is already solved for tau in [0.1204, 0.17227): Majdoddin arXiv:2610.17420 Cor. 10.1 refutes Conj. 5.2/5.7 for all tau<0.17227 and Prop. 10.3 the uMv case for tau1<0.17227. Once fixed, the low-tau part is the same frontier as AS0-02; only the tau~0.53 target is distinct, and that is close to OMv itself.
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
van den Brand, Nanongkai, Saranurak, Dynamic matrix inverse: improved algorithms and matching conditional lower bounds, FOCS 2019
Larsen, Williams, Faster online matrix-vector multiplication, SODA 2017

title: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
W: Malle predicts about X^{1/2} log X quartic fields with Galois group A4 and discriminant up to X. Loughran–Paterson (2025) proved the matching lower bound. The best upper bound is still about X^{0.7785}. Lower the exponent.
M: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/Q with Gal(L~/Q)=A4 and |Delta_L|<=X. Known: X^{1/2} log X << N_{A4}(X) << X^{0.7784...+eps} (Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248 Thm 1.1; BSTTTZ JAMS 2020 Thm 1.4). Prove N_{A4}(X) << X^{beta} for some beta<0.7784 (ideally beta=1/2+eps).
why: A4 is the smallest group whose Malle count is open in both exponent and log-power. The upper bound reduces to bounding 2-torsion in class groups of cyclic cubic fields, so any gain is a gain on ℓ-torsion bounds, the bottleneck in most of Malle's conjecture. Since recent counterexamples hit Türkelli's refined b-constant, the cleanest unrefuted test case should be settled.
notes: red team: Status is accurate: BSTTTZ exponent is .7784..., which LP 2025 cite as the record; no 2026 improvement found (Alberts-Bucur 2602.23619 skips A4). But this is an incremental exponent-lowering target. An upper bound cannot put Malle under pressure, since every outcome is consistent with it. The claim that A4 is the smallest open group is unverified.

title: Optimal dimension dependence in the smoothed complexity of the simplex method
W: Bach and Huiberts (2025) found a simplex method with smoothed complexity O(σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n) pivots and showed σ^{-1/2} is optimal. In the dimension d, the best lower bound is only about d^{1/2}. Close the gap in d.
M: Let D(d,n,sigma) be the expected combinatorial diameter, and S(d,n,sigma) the expected pivot count of the best polynomial-time pivot rule (including Phase I), for {x: Ax<=b} where the rows (a_i,b_i) have norm <=1 before being perturbed by N(0,sigma^2 I). Known: S << sigma^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n, and D >> sigma^{-1/2} d^{1/2} ln(4/sigma)^{-1/4} at n=floor((4/sigma)^d) (Bach-Huiberts). Fix a regime, e.g. sigma<=1/d and log n<=poly(d), and determine the smallest a such that S << sigma^{-1/2} d^{a} polylog(n).
why: Smoothed analysis is the standard explanation for why the simplex method works in practice. With σ-dependence now optimal, the d exponent is the remaining question of whether the explanation is quantitatively sharp. A matching lower bound would come from new constructions of smoothed polytopes with long shadow paths.
notes: red team: Bounds check out against arXiv:2504.04197 (v2, May 2026); no newer improvement in d found. The original M is ill-posed: the d^{1/2} lower bound only holds at n exponential in d, where log n is about d, so the d and log n exponents are tangled. A best simplex method also needs a pivot-rule restriction. Smoothed analysis is a framework, not an unproven assumption.

title: Chaos in the symmetric ABC flow
W: The ABC flow with all three coefficients equal to 1 is the classical steady Euler flow on the 3-torus that is believed to be chaotic. Prove that it really is: show it has positive topological entropy.
M: Prove that the flow of $\dot x=\sin z+\cos y,\ \dot y=\sin x+\cos z,\ \dot z=\sin y+\cos x$ on $\mathbb{T}^3=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$ has positive topological entropy (e.g. by exhibiting a transversal homoclinic orbit to a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or a horseshoe for a Poincare map).
why: The 1:1:1 ABC flow is the standard example of Lagrangian chaos in a steady Beltrami (Euler) flow, and of fast-dynamo and mixing studies since Arnold and Henon. The numerical evidence for chaos since Dombre et al. (1986) is overwhelming, yet only non-integrability (Ziglin) and existence of particular periodic or ballistic orbits are proved. A proof, likely computer-assisted, would close a forty-year gap.
notes: red team: Still open: no proof of positive entropy or a horseshoe at A=B=C=1. Arxiv 2609.17449 (Szumiński–Llibre) is perturbative near the axes only, as the first reviewer said. M is precise. But nobody doubts the answer, and a CAPD or topological-horseshoe proof looks like routine engineering. It is valuable but not elite-deep.

title: Densest k-Subgraph and k-Biclique FPT-inapproximability from plain ETH
W: Prove, assuming only ETH, that Densest k-Subgraph cannot be approximated within k^{o(1)} (or any omega(1) factor) in f(k) n^{o(k)} time, or that k-Biclique has no f(k)n^{o(sqrt k)}-type algorithm, matching known Gap-ETH-based results.
M: Assuming only (deterministic) ETH, prove there is no f(k)*n^{O(1)} algorithm that approximates (uncolored) Densest k-Subgraph within any factor g(k)=omega(1) (Gap-ETH gives k^{o(1)}, Chalermsook et al. FOCS 2017).
why: After Guruswami-Lin-Ren-Sun-Wu (PIH under ETH) and lattice results moving from Gap-ETH to ETH, DkS/k-Biclique are the prominent results still listed only under Gap-ETH.
notes: red team: k-Biclique disjunct already known: Lin (JACM 2018, arXiv:1406.3700) rules out f(k)n^{o(sqrt k)} under ETH (via a probabilistic construction). Constant-factor colored DkS = 2CSP already follows from PIH under ETH (GLRSW). Claim that Aggarwal et al. 2504.02695 lists DkS/k-Biclique as Gap-ETH-only is not in their abstract (a lattice paper); unverified. Remaining part is one item of a broad program.
refs: Guruswami, Lin, Ren, Sun, Wu, Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis under ETH, STOC 2024, arXiv:2311.16587
Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, Zhang, Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness under ETH!, ICALP 2026, arXiv:2504.02695
Chalermsook et al., From Gap-ETH to FPT-inapproximability, FOCS 2017

title: Does 4SUM survive the thin-product attack?
W: Solve 4SUM on n integers of poly(n) magnitude in O(n^{2-eps}) time, or 3SUM-Indexing with S space and T query time where S*T = O(n^{2-eps}); alternatively prove that any algorithm built from AVW-style thin rectangular product subroutines plus fine-grained self-reductions cannot beat n^{ceil(k/2)} for k=4.
M: Yes: the k-SUM hierarchy (and the 3SUM-Indexing data-structure lower bounds) fall, and the n^{ceil(k/2)} conjecture is wrong. A barrier: explains why 3SUM fell but 4SUM did not (lack of self-reductions), and makes 4SUM the natural replacement hardness source.
why: AVW explicitly could not improve k-SUM/k-XOR for k>=4 or 3SUM-Indexing, blaming lack of fine-grained self-reductions. These are now the main surviving additive-combinatorics hypotheses in fine-grained complexity.
notes: red team: Main W is just refuting the 4SUM (k=4 k-SUM) hypothesis itself, so it restates the assumption. The barrier option is undefined ('AVW-style'). Strong 3SUM-Indexing was already refuted (Kopelowitz-Porat; Golovnev et al. 2019), and S*T<n^{2-eps} is a nonstandard form. Status is stale: Chan-Itakura-Ma-Yu (Nov 2026) refute k-SUM for odd k, so only even k is open. AVW claims verified.
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D<=N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026)
Goldstein, Kopelowitz, Lewenstein, Porat, How hard is it to find (honest) witnesses?, ESA 2016 (3SUM-Indexing)

title: From S_2E to E^NP: near-maximum circuit lower bounds
W: Prove E^NP is not contained in SIZE[2^n/n] (or even SIZE[2^{epsilon n}] for some eps>0 infinitely often); equivalently, put Range Avoidance in FP^NP for the relevant circuit classes, improving Li's FS_2^P algorithm.
M: Prove that for some eps>0, E^NP is not contained in SIZE[2^{eps n}], i.e. some L in E^NP has circuit complexity > 2^{eps n} for infinitely many n (stronger: for all large n). Equivalently (Korten 2021), AVOID is in FP^NP.
why: The 2023-24 breakthrough reached S_2E; E^NP is the natural next class and is explicitly the target of the range-avoidance program.
notes: red team: This proves the Klivans-van Melkebeek derandomization assumption rather than putting it under pressure. It is a decades-old headline problem, so it fits the category poorly. Status misses Ren-Williams (ECCC TR26-118, Jul 2026), which shows E^{prMA}/1 needs 2^n/n circuits. Hitchcock (May 2026) verified. The M quantifier 'infinitely often' was ambiguous; fixed.
refs: Chen, Hirahara, Ren, Symmetric exponential time requires near-maximum circuit size, STOC 2024, arXiv:2309.12912
Li, Symmetric exponential time requires near-maximum circuit size: simplified, truly uniform, STOC 2024, arXiv:2310.17762
Hitchcock, Exponential-size circuit complexity is comeager in symmetric exponential time, arXiv:2605.03306
assumption: Circuit lower bounds underlying derandomization (E needs exponential circuits)

title: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
W: Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
M: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that $\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\!\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.
why: Support beyond 2 is the classic test of the symplectic prediction in its non-trivial range and would give better nonvanishing proportions for L(1/2,χ_d). For the averaged family of all Dirichlet characters, Drappeau–Pratt–Radziwiłł got past 2 unconditionally (to 2+50/1093) using large-sieve and dispersion input. The question is whether analogous input exists for the thinner quadratic family.
notes: red team: Still open (no extension past 2 found). The rationale is wrong, though: the symplectic density's nontrivial transition is at support 1, already covered by Ozluk-Snyder/Rubinstein. Past 2 is a technical character-sum barrier, not a test of the symplectic law. It confirms a consequence of Katz-Sarnak rather than pressuring it. Long-known program; B.
assumption: Katz–Sarnak random-matrix symmetry types for low-lying zeros (GRH-based)

title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
M: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.
why: Once the conjecture is false in dimension 3, the main remaining question is how much room counterexamples need. Wang's quadratic theorem and the Bass–Connell–Wright cubic-homogeneous reduction both point to low degree as the decisive regime. Settling $d_3$ means either proving the conjecture for all cubic, quartic or quintic maps in three variables, which would be new even for cubics, or finding a much smaller counterexample. The answer tells us whether the phenomenon is rigid or flexible.
notes: red team: Still open: Gao (rev. Nov 4), van den Essen, Shaska, Migus, Fonollosa and de Bondt (Oct 20) give only degree>=7 maps in dim 3; de Bondt gets degree 3-6 counterexamples only in dims 4-12. No source poses d_3. M is correct, but this is a narrow refinement (JC(3,d) for 3<=d<=6), and bounded-degree search is decidable, so it may be settled by computation soon. Solid B.

title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
W: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
M: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, with a complete proof of both bounds that can be checked (by hand or by a computer computation of feasible size). Sufficient route (Cambie): an explicit $G$ with $\alpha(G)\le2$, $|V(G)|=4t-1$ and no connected matching of size $t$ (a matching whose edges are pairwise joined by an edge of $G$) violates Hadwiger's conjecture.
why: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943) is one of the central problems of graph theory, generalizing the Four Colour Theorem; a disproof would reshape the theory of minors and colouring. A non-constructive counterexample of tower-like size tells us little about where the conjecture fails, while an explicit moderate-size one would be checkable, would independently confirm the claim, and would show which structures (e.g. dense graphs with independence number 2, Seymour's test case) actually break it.
notes: red team: Premise confirmed: Family 157 of OpenAI's Oct 2026 release, surveyed in arXiv 2610.17090, is non-explicit, not peer reviewed and unverified. M's 'Equivalently decide min<10^6' is false (deciding includes the hopeless negative half), so I removed it. The 10^6 cutoff is arbitrary and the problem rests on an unverified claim. FGS is known for t<=22, so this route needs n>=91. B.

title: Which monodromy groups do Jacobian counterexamples have?
W: A Keller map (polynomial map with constant nonzero Jacobian) that is not invertible covers a generic point d times, and following the d preimages around loops gives a permutation group, its monodromy. Campbell's 1973 theorem says that if this group is regular (the Galois case), the map is invertible. The 2026 counterexamples realize full symmetric groups and some imprimitive groups. Is Campbell's theorem the only obstruction?
M: For a Keller map $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ ($\det JF\in\mathbb C^\times$) of geometric degree $d\ge2$, let $\mathrm{Mon}(F)\le S_d$ be the geometric monodromy group (Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x)/\mathbb C(F)$ acting on the $d$ embeddings). It is transitive, and by Campbell's theorem it is regular only if $d=1$. Let $\mathcal M$ be the set of transitive groups (up to permutation isomorphism) arising as $\mathrm{Mon}(F)$ for non-invertible Keller maps in some dimension; $\mathcal M$ contains $S_d$, $A_d$ (e.g. $d=6,12$ and the families of Kistner-Shaska 2608.02863) and imprimitive wreath-type groups (Fonollosa 2609.33491), and is closed under direct products in product action ($F\times G$). Is $\mathcal M$ exactly the set of non-regular transitive groups? Test case: does some primitive group not containing $A_d$ (e.g. $\mathrm{AGL}(1,p)$ for a prime $p\ge5$, or $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ on 7 points) lie in $\mathcal M$? Equivalently, is every primitive member of $\mathcal M$ alternating or symmetric?
why: Since the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in 2026, the field has produced dozens of explicit counterexamples, and monodromy is the invariant used to tell them apart (S_3 for Alpöge's map, S_N for weighted lifts, the imprimitive groups G_n of marked-root maps of order m^n n!/gcd(2,m)). The geometric degree question is settled: every d >= 3 occurs. Monodromy is the next coarse invariant, and it is not settled. The only general constraint is Campbell's Galois theorem, together with older two-dimensional Galois-theoretic results (Razar, Wright). An inverse-Galois-type classification would say exactly how much of the classical Galois approach to the conjecture was ever viable. A new obstruction (for example, that alternating groups never occur) would be a structural theorem about étale maps of affine space.
notes: red team: Proposed decisive test case is already answered: Kistner-Shaska (2608.02863, in reviewer's own refs) prove geometric monodromy A_12 (Thm 5.5), A_6, A_N for k even (Thm 6.1), A_{2r-1} (Thm 6.5). W and why wrongly omit alternating groups. Full inverse problem is still open but no paper poses it and it is inverse-Galois-scale with no visible path. Fixed M uses a primitive non-A_d test.

title: Maximal eigenfunction growth beyond surfaces of revolution
W: On the round sphere, some eigenfunctions are as peaked as theory allows, because every geodesic leaving the pole comes back to it. Sogge and Zelditch proved that on any real-analytic surface, maximally peaked eigenfunctions force such a 'pole'. Is rotational symmetry also forced: must such a surface be a surface of revolution?
M: Let $(M,g)$ be a compact boundaryless real-analytic Riemannian surface with $\Delta_g e_j=-\lambda_j^2e_j$, $\|e_j\|_{L^2}=1$. Say $g$ has maximal eigenfunction growth if $\limsup_j \|e_j\|_{L^\infty}/\lambda_j^{1/2}>0$ for some orthonormal eigenbasis. Decide whether every such $(M,g)$ admits a nontrivial isometric $S^1$-action, i.e. is a surface of revolution. (Necessary condition, Sogge-Zelditch 2016: $M$ has a pole $p$, meaning all geodesics from $p$ return smoothly closed at a common time $2T_p$.)
why: Sogge–Zelditch showed that a real-analytic surface has maximal eigenfunction growth only if it has a pole. Proving that explicit surfaces have no pole is the missing step for concrete examples; the triaxial ellipsoid is already done.
notes: Replaces the arbitrary Fermat-quartic instance with the open question stated in Sogge-Zelditch II (1409.2063, Rev. Mat. Iberoam.).
